title: The Step of the Omnibus at Coutances: the Fuchsian Functions, the Recalled Memoir, and the Measure of Time
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nancy, the house opposite the ducal palace
stops.date_confidence: date attested (MacTutor, biography of Poincaré; Académie française notice). Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 48.6934/6.1817 for a supposed Cité Ducale birthplace, roughly 400 m too far south. Lebon (Gutenberg 32948) places the birth house facing the ducal palace, which fr.wikipedia pins at 48.69694/6.18028, and the palace and the rue de Guise stand in the Ville-Vieille, not in a quarter called Cité ducale; that phrase is en.wikipedia's and is not reproduced here. The exact street number, commonly given as 2 rue de Guise, is not geocoded to a building.
stops.campa: In a house facing the ducal palace of the old town, Eugénie Launois bears a son to the physician Léon Poincaré, who teaches in the medical faculty. They name him Jules Henri. The household is Lorraine professional bourgeoisie: consultations, books, a good address, a sister born two years later. A cousin born a dozen years after him, Raymond, will govern France. This one is born with weak eyesight and an awkward body, and he will never in his life be able to draw a figure that anyone else can read.
suggested_refs: The Poincaré birth house facing the Palais ducal, Nancy, marked by a commemorative plaque
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré
Ernest Lebon, Henri Poincaré, Project Gutenberg 32948

stops.name: Nancy, the diphtheria and the five months
stops.date_confidence: attested, and upgraded here from the reconstruction the pool first offered: fr.wikipedia states he contracted diphtheria at five, that is in 1859, with a paralysis of about five months, not merely a temporary one. Month and day are nowhere recorded and default to 01-01. The mother's bedside teaching during the convalescence is the traditional account, carried in the biographical literature rather than in a document.
stops.campa: At five the diphtheria takes his throat and then his legs. The paralysis holds about five months. He cannot speak through it; he learns to follow talk he is unable to join, and his mother sits with him and teaches him there. What comes out of the sickroom is a child who does his work in his head because his hands will not serve him. He keeps the habit at fifty: problems turned over while walking, on stairs, at the table, and set down on paper only once they are finished.
suggested_refs: The traditional account of the 1859 illness in the French biographical literature on Poincaré
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré
Times of London obituary, reprinted at mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/TimesObituaries/Poincare/

stops.name: Nancy, eleven years at the lycée
stops.date_confidence: year attested (MacTutor: 'In 1862, Henri entered the Lycée in Nancy'; Académie française notice; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Month and day not recorded; October is the ordinary start of the French school year and is used here as an ordering device. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 48.6903/6.1796 to the school's own, 48° 41' 28" N 6° 10' 42" E per fr.wikipedia, entrance at 2 rue de la Visitation. The two baccalaureates of 1871 are attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia entry.
stops.campa: He enters the lycée of Nancy and stays eleven years. He takes first prizes in French and Latin composition as readily as in mathematics, and a teacher's phrase for him, a monster of mathematics, gets around the town. He reads at an extraordinary rate and forgets nothing he has read. In 1871, the year after the Prussians came down into Lorraine, he passes the baccalaureate in letters and then the one in science. The school takes his name in 1913, the year after he dies.
suggested_refs: The Lycée Henri-Poincaré, 2 rue de la Visitation, Nancy, renamed for him in 1913
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Nancy, the ambulance rounds of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested that he served for a time in the ambulance corps alongside his physician father during the Franco-Prussian War (Times of London obituary, reprinted at mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk). No month is recorded; August 1870, the month the French armies broke in Lorraine, is an ordering device. Coordinate is central Nancy, not a specific dressing station, none being named in any source reached.
stops.campa: The Prussian armies come down into Lorraine and Nancy falls under occupation. Poincaré is sixteen and still at the lycée. He goes out with his father on the ambulance rounds, and what he sees is the medical aftermath of a defeat, the wounded of an army that has already broken, carried in from the country around the town. The Times of London, forty-two years later, will compress the whole of it into a single line: he served for a time in the Ambulance Corps. Of what he made of it at the time nothing survives in his own hand.
suggested_refs: The Times of London obituary of Henri Poincaré, 17 July 1912
sources: Times of London obituary, reprinted at mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/TimesObituaries/Poincare/
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Paris, first in the competition for the Polytechnique
stops.date_confidence: attested that he entered the École polytechnique in 1873 placing first in the entrance competition, and graduated in 1875 ranked second (MacTutor; Académie française notice). Month and day not recorded; October is the ordinary start of the school year. The coordinate is the canonical atlas pin for the old Polytechnique on the rue Descartes, inherited byte-identically from evariste_galois.journey.json and augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json. The attribution of his second place to weak draughtsmanship is carried from the research pool's geography lens rather than from a graded record.
stops.campa: He sits the entrance competition for the École polytechnique and comes out first in France. The school on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève trains the state's engineers and its artillery officers, and it grades drawing. Poincaré cannot draw. Over two years of ranking he loses ground steadily on the descriptive-geometry benches and graduates second, beaten by a hand he does not have. Classmates remember him solving problems without notes and answering questions before the questioner has finished asking them.
suggested_refs: The old École polytechnique on the rue Descartes, Montagne Sainte-Geneviève
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Paris, the École des mines on the boulevard Saint-Michel
stops.date_confidence: attested: 'From November 1875 to June 1878 he studied at the École des Mines' (en.wikipedia, 'Henri Poincaré'), corroborated by MacTutor. Day within November not recorded and defaults to 01. His first mathematical paper, on the properties of the indicatrix of a surface (1874), is tagged R in the pool's chronology lens and is not given a stop of its own here.
stops.campa: From November 1875 to June 1878 he studies at the École des mines on the boulevard Saint-Michel, the school that turns the top of the Polytechnique list into the Corps des mines, the most closed engineering body in France. He works the curriculum: mineralogy, ventilation, the law of concessions. Beside it, in the evenings and on his own account, he does mathematics nobody has assigned him, and by the last year he has a doctoral subject. He leaves in June 1878 qualified as a mining engineer.
suggested_refs: The École des mines, 60 boulevard Saint-Michel, Paris
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré
Annales des mines archival dossier, annales.org/archives/x/hpoincar.html

stops.name: Vesoul, the mineralogical sub-district
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Times obituary has him acting 'for a short time as mining engineer at Vesoul', and the Annales des mines dossier (annales.org/archives/x/hpoincar.html) documents the posting to the Vesoul sub-district in the spring of 1879. Day within March not recorded and defaults to 01. The six-month duration is the pool's geography lens, consistent with the December 1879 move to Caen.
stops.campa: Qualified into the Corps des mines, he is posted to the mineralogical sub-district of Vesoul, in the Haute-Saône, as inspecting engineer. The district is a small one: the coal at Ronchamp, some quarries, a few works. He rides out to inspections, writes his reports, and carries on with the thesis he has been building for two years. The Corps expects a working engineer and for six months he is one. Nothing in the record says he disliked the posting, and nothing says he meant to stay in it.
suggested_refs: The Corps des mines service record of Henri Poincaré, Annales des mines archive
sources: Times of London obituary, reprinted at mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/TimesObituaries/Poincare/
Annales des mines archival dossier, annales.org/archives/x/hpoincar.html

stops.name: Paris, the thesis before Hermite and Darboux
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 August 1879 (MacTutor; Sorbonne heritage library digitized thesis record, patrimoine.sorbonne-universite.fr/idurl/1/1607). Coordinate is the canonical atlas Sorbonne pin, 47 rue des Écoles, inherited byte-identically from marie_curie.journey.json, whose own file records that the research material repeatedly gave the Panthéon's latitude for the Sorbonne. Darboux's remark that the thesis held enough for several dissertations is carried from MacTutor and is a reported judgement, not a minuted one.
stops.campa: On the first of August he defends 'Sur les propriétés des fonctions définies par les équations aux différences partielles' before a jury that includes Gaston Darboux and Charles Hermite. Darboux, examining, finds the candidate has proved a great deal more than was needed and left the proofs unpolished, and judges that there is material here for several good dissertations. Hermite has been steering him since the Polytechnique. Poincaré is twenty-five and now, on paper, a mining engineer and a doctor of mathematical sciences at once.
suggested_refs: The digitized thesis record, Sorbonne heritage library, patrimoine.sorbonne-universite.fr/idurl/1/1607
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Ronchamp, down the shaft at Magny
stops.date_confidence: date and death toll corrected here against the pool's own chronology lens, which gave August 1879 and eighteen dead from en.wikipedia. Both French sources agree on sixteen and on 1 September 1879: annales.org ('une explosion de grisou avait fait 16 victimes') and fr.wikipedia ('1er septembre 1879 dans le Puits du Magny, causant la mort de seize mineurs'). The en.wikipedia figure is the weaker witness on both counts and is not followed. Coordinate is the Ronchamp basin, not the individual shaft head.
stops.campa: On the first of September firedamp explodes in the Puits du Magny near Ronchamp and sixteen miners are killed. Poincaré, the district's engineer, goes down the shaft himself while the workings are still burning, and then conducts the official technical inquiry: where the gas gathered, how the lamps were kept, what the ventilation did and failed to do. He is the man the state sends underground to establish what happened. Three months after signing the report he leaves the field for a lecture room in Normandy.
suggested_refs: The Puits du Magny, Ronchamp coalfield, and the 1 September 1879 firedamp inquiry
sources: Annales des mines archival dossier, annales.org/archives/x/hpoincar.html

stops.name: Caen, the lectureship in analysis
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1879 (MacTutor; en.wikipedia; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Day not recorded and defaults to 01. The Académie des sciences Grand Prix des sciences mathématiques of 1880, on the theory of linear differential equations, is the competition into which his first supplements went; the pool's chronology lens dated the Fuchsian breakthrough to 1881, which is too late, and it is placed here at 1880 with the Acta Mathematica papers following in 1882.
stops.campa: He is appointed junior lecturer in mathematical analysis at the Faculty of Sciences of Caen. It is a provincial post at the bottom of the ladder, the calculus taught to Norman students, and he holds it for less than two years. There is no library here worth the word, and nobody within reach is working anywhere near his problems. The Academy of Sciences has just announced its Grand Prix for 1880, on the theory of linear differential equations. He enters, and over the next two years sends in a memoir and three supplements.
suggested_refs: The Académie des sciences Grand Prix des sciences mathématiques memoir of 1880 and its three supplements
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Caen, a fortnight of failure and a night of black coffee
stops.date_confidence: the episode is Poincaré's own retrospective testimony, given in the 1908 lecture on mathematical invention and printed in Science and Method; the quotation is verified verbatim in the Halsted translation of The Foundations of Science, Project Gutenberg 39713. He supplies no date. It belongs to the Caen period and to the 1880 Grand Prix work, and February 1880 is an ordering device only. The naming of the functions after Lazarus Fuchs is attested; Fuchs's own priority in them is precisely what Klein will dispute the following year.
stops.campa: He is working at equations he cannot solve, trying for a fortnight to prove that functions of the kind he wants cannot exist. The proof will not come. One evening, against his own habit, he drinks black coffee and does not sleep, and the ideas rise all night and collide until pairs of them lock together. By morning he has established the existence of one whole class of the functions he had been trying to rule out. He names them Fuchsian, after Lazarus Fuchs, whose papers had set him on them. Writing it up takes a few hours.
stops.quote: For fifteen days I strove to prove that there could not be any functions like those I have since called Fuchsian functions... One evening, contrary to my custom, I drank black coffee and could not sleep. Ideas rose in crowds; I felt them collide until pairs interlocked, so to speak, making a stable combination.
stops.quote_source: Henri Poincaré, 'Mathematical Creation,' in Science and Method, in The Foundations of Science, trans. George Bruce Halsted, Project Gutenberg 39713
suggested_refs: Poincaré's lecture 'L'invention mathématique' to the Société de psychologie, 1908
sources: Project Gutenberg 39713, The Foundations of Science, Halsted translation
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Coutances, the step of the omnibus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. The episode is Poincaré's own first-person testimony in Science and Method, verified verbatim in the Halsted translation, and it carries no year; MacTutor reproduces it and assigns none. The pool's geography lens dated it c. 1881, which sits after the Caen year's decisive work; it belongs with the geological excursion of the Caen period and the 1880 supplements, and June 1880 is an ordering device. The [R] tag on uncorroborated first-person recollection stands.
stops.campa: A geological excursion takes the party to Coutances. There is an omnibus waiting to carry them somewhere, and as he puts his foot on the step, with nothing in his head that leads to it, he sees that the transformations he had used to define the Fuchsian functions are identical with those of non-Euclidean geometry. He does not check it. He gets in, goes on with the conversation he was having, and verifies the whole thing at leisure after he is back in Caen, where it holds.
stops.quote: Having reached Coutances, we entered an omnibus to go some place or other. At the moment when I put my foot on the step the idea came to me, without anything in my former thoughts seeming to have paved the way for it, that the transformations I had used to define the Fuchsian functions were identical with those of non-Euclidean geometry.
stops.quote_source: Henri Poincaré, 'Mathematical Creation,' in Science and Method, in The Foundations of Science, trans. George Bruce Halsted, Project Gutenberg 39713
suggested_refs: Science and Method, Book I, chapter III, on mathematical creation
sources: Project Gutenberg 39713, The Foundations of Science, Halsted translation
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Caen, the marriage to Louise Poulain d'Andecy
stops.date_confidence: the date, 20 April 1881, is attested by both the Stanford Encyclopedia entry and en.wikipedia. The PLACE is contradicted between them and the contradiction is not resolved here: en.wikipedia puts the wedding at Caen, where they met, and the pool's chronology lens gives Paris on the same day. Caen is used for the pin because it is the reading that was independently checked, and the conflict is recorded rather than adjudicated. The descent of Louise's mother from the Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire naturalists is attested by en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: He marries Louise Poulain d'Andecy, whose mother's line goes back to the naturalists Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire. He is twenty-seven and has been a lecturer for sixteen months. Four children follow, three daughters and a son. Of the marriage almost nothing is on the public record, and not a letter between them has been printed. She will outlive him by twenty-two years. The sources do not agree on which town the wedding was in: one puts it at Caen, where the couple met, another at Paris on the same day.
suggested_refs: The contradictory Caen and Paris accounts of the 20 April 1881 marriage

stops.name: Caen, the letters going to Leipzig
stops.date_confidence: attested that Klein and Poincaré corresponded and competed over automorphic functions and uniformization through 1881-82 (MacTutor, biography of Felix Klein; felix_klein.journey.json, stop 'Leipzig, the race with Poincaré and the collapse'). The opening month is placed at June 1881, when Klein wrote first after the Comptes rendus notes; the exact letter count is not fixed by any source reached and the figure given in the campa is approximate. Klein's collapse in the autumn of 1882 is attested in his own file and its sources.
stops.campa: Felix Klein, seven years older and already professor at Leipzig, writes to Caen. He has read the notes on Fuchsian functions in the Comptes rendus and objects, among other things, to the name: Fuchs did not do this work, and Klein has. What follows runs a year and a half, courteous and steadily harder, each man driving toward a general uniformization theorem and using the other as a pacemaker. Poincaré answers the objection about naming by attaching Klein's name to a second class of functions. In the autumn of 1882 Klein breaks down and his research never resumes.
suggested_refs: The Klein-Poincaré correspondence of 1881-82 on automorphic functions and uniformization
Poincaré, 'Théorie des groupes fuchsiens', Acta Mathematica 1 (1882)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Felix Klein

segments.name: The Paris Chairs and King Oscar's Prize

stops.name: Paris, maître de conférences d'analyse
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1881 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; MacTutor). Day not recorded and defaults to 01. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Sorbonne pin inherited from marie_curie.journey.json. The Acta Mathematica papers on Fuchsian groups are dated 1882 per en.wikipedia, 'Fuchsian group'.
stops.campa: He leaves Caen for the Faculty of Sciences in Paris as maître de conférences d'analyse, twenty-two months after arriving in Normandy. He is twenty-seven. From this year until his death he holds no post outside the city, and everything that follows happens within a few kilometres of the Latin Quarter: the Sorbonne, the Polytechnique, the Institut on the quai Conti, the Observatory, a flat on the rue Claude-Bernard. The mature papers on Fuchsian groups reach Acta Mathematica the year after he arrives.
suggested_refs: The Faculty of Sciences of the University of Paris, 47 rue des Écoles
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Paris, analysis at the Polytechnique
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1883 (Académie française notice; MacTutor). Month and day not recorded and default to 01-01. The tenure to 1897 is carried from the pool's interlock lens. Coordinate is the canonical atlas pin for the old Polytechnique on the rue Descartes. The list of published lecture volumes is a compressed characterization of the Cours de la Faculté des sciences and the Polytechnique courses rather than a titled bibliography.
stops.campa: He begins teaching analysis at the École polytechnique, on the same rue Descartes site where he sat the entrance competition ten years before, and keeps the course while holding his Sorbonne duties. Later he adds the Bureau des longitudes and the school of posts and telegraphs to the load. The published lecture volumes run to a dozen and more: capillarity, elasticity, optics, thermodynamics, potential theory, the mathematics of electricity. He teaches whatever he is working on, so the courses change from year to year.
suggested_refs: The published Cours of Henri Poincaré, Gauthier-Villars, from the Sorbonne and Polytechnique lectures
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Poincaré

stops.name: Paris, the chair of mathematical physics and probability
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1886, succeeding Gabriel Lippmann (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; en.wikipedia). Month and day not recorded and default to 01-01. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Sorbonne pin. That he never worked in a laboratory is a characterization consistent with every source reached but is nowhere stated as such in them.
stops.campa: He succeeds Gabriel Lippmann in the Paris chair of mathematical physics and probability and holds it until he dies. The chair obliges a different branch of physics each year, and he obliges it: optics, electricity, thermodynamics, capillarity, the theory of Maxwell, teaching himself the field in the months before he teaches it to anyone else. He does the learning on paper. No source reached here puts him at a bench, or in a laboratory, or running an experiment of his own.
stops.quote: Science is built up with facts, as a house is with stones. But a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house.
stops.quote_source: Henri Poincaré, Science and Hypothesis, in The Foundations of Science, trans. George Bruce Halsted, Project Gutenberg 39713
suggested_refs: The Sorbonne chair of mathematical physics and calculus of probabilities, held 1886-1912
sources: Project Gutenberg 39713, The Foundations of Science

stops.name: Paris, the Institut de France, elected at thirty-two
stops.date_confidence: date attested (Times of London obituary; en.wikipedia). He was thirty-two, the Times obituary saying thirty-three, which is an error in a source otherwise relied on here. The claim in the pool's geography lens that he was the only member ever associated with every mathematical and physical section of the Academy could not be confirmed against any source reached and is dropped rather than carried. His presidency of the Academy in 1906 is attested by the Académie française notice.
stops.campa: At thirty-two he is elected to the Academy of Sciences in the geometry section, at an age when most candidates have not yet been proposed. He will belong to it for twenty-five years and preside over it in 1906. The Institut sits on the quai Conti under the dome that Mazarin's legacy paid for, and he will be elected into the building a second time, in 1908, by the other academy that meets there. The Times of London, reporting his death, gets his age at this election wrong by a year.
suggested_refs: The Institut de France, quai Conti, seat of the Académie des sciences and the Académie française
sources: Times of London obituary, reprinted at mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/TimesObituaries/Poincare/

stops.name: Paris, the memoir for King Oscar's competition
stops.date_confidence: the competition was announced in Acta Mathematica in 1885, not 1887 as MacTutor implies, per actamathematica.org/library/prize-competition; entries were due in 1888. The submission day is not recorded and 1 June is an ordering device. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Paris pin. The motto Nunquam praescriptos transibunt sidera fines is the one attached to his entry in the standard accounts of the competition.
stops.campa: King Oscar II of Sweden has offered a prize for his sixtieth birthday, announced in Acta Mathematica three years earlier by Gösta Mittag-Leffler, with four set questions. The first asks for the stability of the solar system, in the form of a convergent series expansion for the n-body problem. Poincaré does not answer it. He submits instead a memoir on the restricted three-body problem, under the motto Nunquam praescriptos transibunt sidera fines, which gives up the search for solutions in favour of the qualitative geometry of every possible trajectory.
suggested_refs: The Acta Mathematica prize competition of King Oscar II, announced 1885
sources: June Barrow-Green, Poincaré and the Three Body Problem (1997), as summarized there

stops.name: Paris, the prize from the hands of the Swedish ambassador
stops.date_confidence: corrected against the pool's own chronology and geography lenses, which both placed this in Stockholm. Poincaré never went. Per actamathematica.org/library/prize-competition the result was announced 20 January 1889, the day before the King's sixtieth birthday, and 'he received his prize from the Swedish ambassador in Paris in March 1889'. Day within March not recorded and defaults to 01. Weierstrass's judgement that the memoir opens a new era is attested in the same source and in the Times obituary's shorter notice of the prize.
stops.campa: The jury, Mittag-Leffler with Karl Weierstrass and Charles Hermite, awards him the prize on the twentieth of January, the day before the King's sixtieth birthday. Weierstrass writes that the memoir does not solve the problem that was set, and that its publication will all the same open a new era in celestial mechanics. Poincaré does not go to Sweden. In March the Swedish ambassador in Paris hands him the gold medal and two thousand five hundred kronor, and the memoir goes to the printers in Stockholm.
suggested_refs: Weierstrass's report on the prize memoir, Acta Mathematica prize competition papers
sources: Times of London obituary, reprinted at mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/TimesObituaries/Poincare/

stops.name: Paris, the telegram to stop the presses
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The pool's chronology, geography, and afterlife lenses all state that Phragmén found the error; he did not. Per actamathematica.org/library/prize-competition his persistent questions about the convergence of infinite series prompted Poincaré to re-examine the memoir, and Poincaré found his own mistake, that he had assumed the asymptotic surfaces were closed, and telegraphed Mittag-Leffler on 30 November 1889 to stop the presses. The figures, over 3,500 kronor against a 2,500-kronor prize, are documented in the same source.
stops.campa: Lars Edvard Phragmén, editing the memoir for Acta Mathematica, keeps asking about the convergence of certain infinite series. The questions are not objections; they are questions. Poincaré goes back into the argument to answer them and finds his own mistake there: he had assumed the asymptotic surfaces were closed, and they are not. On the thirtieth of November he telegraphs Mittag-Leffler to stop the presses. Copies have already gone out. The recall and reprinting cost him over three thousand five hundred kronor against a prize of two thousand five hundred.
suggested_refs: The two surviving copies of the suppressed first printing at the Institut Mittag-Leffler, one annotated 'The whole edition was destroyed. M.L.'
sources: June Barrow-Green, Poincaré and the Three Body Problem (1997)

stops.name: Paris, the corrected memoir and the theorem of return
stops.date_confidence: attested: the corrected memoir appeared in December 1890 in Acta Mathematica vol. 13 (actamathematica.org/library/prize-competition). Day not recorded and defaults to 01. The recurrence theorem is standardly attributed to the same 1890 work. The quotation is verified verbatim in the Halsted translation, Project Gutenberg 39713, and is from the essay 'Chance' in Science and Method, written some years later; it is placed here because it is the passage in which he states the sensitivity that the corrected memoir had forced on him.
stops.campa: The corrected memoir appears in December 1890, half as long again as the version that was destroyed. What replaced the error is the tangle: stable and unstable asymptotic curves crossing each other infinitely often, in a figure he declines to attempt to draw and whose complexity, he writes, he will not even try to describe. The same work carries the recurrence theorem, that a bounded system preserving volume must come back arbitrarily close to any state it has held. Two copies of the destroyed printing survive at the Institut Mittag-Leffler.
stops.quote: A very slight cause, which escapes us, determines a considerable effect which we can not help seeing, and then we say this effect is due to chance.
stops.quote_source: Henri Poincaré, 'Chance,' in Science and Method, in The Foundations of Science, trans. George Bruce Halsted, Project Gutenberg 39713
suggested_refs: Poincaré, 'Sur le problème des trois corps et les équations de la dynamique', Acta Mathematica 13 (1890)
Les méthodes nouvelles de la mécanique céleste, 3 vols., 1892-1899
sources: Project Gutenberg 39713, The Foundations of Science

segments.name: Longitudes, Situs, and the Measure of Time

stops.name: Paris Observatory, the Bureau des longitudes
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1893 for both the Bureau des longitudes and the promotion to chief engineer in the Corps des mines (Académie française notice; en.wikipedia). Month and day not recorded and default to 01-01. The description of the Bureau's work on telegraphic longitude is standard institutional history and is the ground on which Peter Galison's Einstein's Clocks, Poincaré's Maps reads the 1898 paper; that reading is cited in the research dossier but was not independently re-fetched.
stops.campa: He is elected to the Bureau des longitudes, and is promoted chief engineer in the Corps des mines in the same year. The Bureau is where French time is made. It fixes longitudes by telegraph, which is to say it fixes what it means for a clock in Paris and a clock in Dakar to read the same hour, and the answer it gives is that a signal is sent, and its travel time is halved, and the halving is a stipulation. The Bureau's minutes for the years after put him on geodesy, chronometry, and the transmission of time signals.
suggested_refs: Peter Galison, Einstein's Clocks, Poincaré's Maps (2003), on the Bureau des longitudes and telegraphic simultaneity

stops.name: Paris, Analysis Situs
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1895, with the first topology papers dated 1894-95 (MacTutor). Month and day not recorded and default to 01-01. Coordinate is the canonical atlas Sorbonne pin. The five supplements ran to 1904; the fifth is where the false homological claim is replaced by the question later called the Poincaré conjecture. The quotation is verified verbatim in the Halsted translation and comes from 'The Future of Mathematics' in Science and Method, correcting the essay attribution given in the research pool.
stops.campa: He publishes Analysis Situs in the Journal de l'École polytechnique: a hundred and twenty pages that invent a subject. Homology, the fundamental group, Betti numbers, the classification of manifolds by invariants that survive any continuous deformation. He is asking what is left of a shape when measurement is taken away from it, and the answer turns out to be a great deal, enough to tell a sphere from a torus without measuring either one. Five supplements follow over the next decade, in two of which he corrects himself in public.
stops.quote: Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things.

stops.campa: In the Revue de métaphysique et de morale he publishes 'La mesure du temps'. There is no such thing, he argues, as a simultaneity between distant events that is directly given to anybody. To say that two things happened at once in Paris and in Berlin is to have already adopted a rule, ordinarily the rule that light takes the same time to travel each way along a line, and that rule is chosen because it makes the equations simple, not because it has been verified. The Bureau des longitudes had been doing precisely this with cables for five years.

stops.name: Paris, the petition of January 1898
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. stops.campa: The Dreyfus case is four years old and Zola's J'accuse has just come out in L'Aurore. A petition goes round among academics and writers asking only that the judicial irregularities of 1894 be examined, and Poincaré signs it. He is not a political man and does not become one. What he has to bring to the affair is narrower and harder than a signature: he holds a chair in the calculus of probabilities, and the case against Alfred Dreyfus rests on a probability argument.

stops.name: Paris, the letter to the council of war at Rennes
stops.date_confidence: attested that he addressed a letter to the council of war at Rennes in 1899 (fr.wikipedia, 'Henri Poincaré': 'En 1899, Henri Poincaré adresse une lettre au Conseil de guerre de Rennes'). Month and day are not recorded; August is the month the retrial opened and is an ordering device. The pool's geography lens said Paul Painlevé read the letter into the record; nothing reached confirms that, and it is dropped. The Edinburgh dossier, which the pool cited here, was fetched and says nothing about 1899, Painlevé, or Bertillon. The stop stays in Paris: Rennes belongs to those who were in the courtroom.
stops.campa: The court-martial reconvenes at Rennes and Alphonse Bertillon appears again with his system, which holds that the incriminating bordereau was self-forged by Dreyfus on a redrawn grid, and that the coincidences to be counted in it are too improbable to be accidental. Poincaré does not go to Rennes. He writes to the council of war instead and takes the calculation apart on its own ground: the coincidences are not independent, the probability is computed after the fact on the very data that suggested it, and nothing at all follows. Dreyfus is convicted a second time.

The report finds the reasoning devoid of any scientific value whatever, and says why in terms a court can follow: an argument that assigns probabilities with no prior, on a hypothesis chosen because the data fit it, and that compares a document only against itself, is not a calculation. In July 1906 the conviction is annulled and Dreyfus is reinstated in the army.
stops.quote: To doubt everything and to believe everything are two equally convenient solutions; each saves us from thinking.

Its argument is that the axioms of geometry are neither truths known in advance nor experimental facts, but disguised definitions, conventions adopted for convenience, and that a good deal of mechanics is in the same position. Euclidean geometry is not true. It is convenient, and it will remain in use for exactly as long as it remains convenient. Within three years the book is in English and in German; the English is W. J. Greenstreet's, published in London with a preface by Joseph Larmor.

stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic, which he seldom does, for the International Congress of Arts and Science held with the World's Fair in Forest Park. His address is 'The Principles of Mathematical Physics'. In it he states a principle of relativity: the laws of physics must be the same for an observer at rest and for one carried along in uniform translation, so that no experiment can disclose an absolute motion. He describes the local time of Lorentz as what clocks synchronized by light signals would actually read, and allows that the ether may be a hypothesis due to be discarded.

stops.name: Paris, Académie des sciences, sur la dynamique de l'électron

stops.campa: He presents a five-page note to the Academy, 'Sur la dynamique de l'électron'. It corrects an error in Lorentz's transformation equations, gives those equations Lorentz's name, and shows that they form a group: two of them applied in succession compose into a third of the same family, which is what makes the principle of relativity exact rather than approximate. He proposes as well that gravitation propagates at the speed of light. Twenty-five days later, in Bern, Albert Einstein posts a paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies.

stops.campa: The Circolo Matematico di Palermo receives the long version, sixty pages where the note to the Academy had five. Poincaré works in four dimensions, takes time as a fourth coordinate with an imaginary factor so that the Lorentz group becomes a group of rotations in a four-dimensional space, and writes down the invariant interval. He looks for a law of gravitation that will fit inside the same structure. The paper is printed in the Rendiconti the following January, in French, on Italian pages, and for a long time very few people read it.

He gives that audience his own case, in order: the fortnight of failure, the coffee, the step of the omnibus at Coutances. What he builds on it is that the unconscious does the combining, and that the conscious mind only chooses among what it is handed, by a criterion he says is aesthetic before it is logical. Psychologists have read the lecture more often than mathematicians since.
